summary: All of this bot's text-generation traffic now reaches Router through one change: the single AsyncOpenAI client in OpenAIHelper.__init__ is wrapped with the vendored runtime, so the four chat.completions sites (a user's chat turn, its streamed twin, the plugin function-call loop, and history summarisation) are translated to Router's /v1/responses and served by the catalog's gpt-4o at the same list price, falling back to OpenAI untouched whenever RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY is absent or Router refuses before generating. gpt-4o, the default and the vision model, is a catalog id, so no model substitution and no behaviour change was needed anywhere: five driven paths (chat, streamed chat, summarise, vision, streamed vision) each produced a valid Router request against the simulator and the app's own assertions passed. Image generation, text-to-speech and Whisper transcription stay on the OpenAI key because Router serves no endpoint for them; nothing the bot could do before has been lost. Three improvements are built on branches (cross-vendor fallbacks plus a provider timeout on the chat path, a cheap model for summarisation, a per-conversation prompt cache key) and four more are proposed for a human to approve.
reviewed: Read every LLM call in bot/openai_helper.py and how bot/telegram_bot.py waits on it (each of the four chat sites sits directly in a Telegram reply the user is watching), plus bot/usage_tracker.py's cost model and bot/main.py's configuration surface. The proposals that stop short of a branch are the ones that change observable behaviour or need a product call: billing users from Router's exact cost instead of a flat TOKEN_PRICE, replacing the hard-coded 2024 OpenAI model tables with the live catalog, porting the chat path to Responses natively, and two configuration settings that silently take all chat traffic off Router. The plugins (bot/plugins/*) call third-party HTTP APIs, not LLMs, so nothing there was worth proposing.

items.title: Route the shared OpenAI client
items.summary: The one AsyncOpenAI client is wrapped with the Router runtime, so all four chat.completions sites are served by Router as /v1/responses.
items.gains: One key and one gateway for every text generation the bot does, with per-request spend labels already carrying the calling function (bot/openai_helper.py:__common_get_chat_response and the other three), and per-request provider fallback: if Router refuses before generating, the original request goes to OpenAI once.
items.price: no change: gpt-4o is a catalog id at $2.50/$10 per 1M tokens, the same list price OpenAI charges, and the model is unchanged, so answers are unchanged
items.why: Every one of these four calls is a user sitting in a Telegram chat waiting for a reply, and they all share one client built once in OpenAIHelper.__init__. Wrapping that constructor is therefore the whole migration: no call-site edits, no request-shape changes, and the app behaves exactly as before until RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY is set. The default model (gpt-4o) and the vision model (gpt-4o) are both in Router's catalog with tools and image input, so nothing had to be substituted or ported; the runtime translates the legacy `functions` payload the plugin system still sends, and drops nothing the app relies on. The alternative, pointing the client's base_url at Router, would have cost the per-request provider fallback and would have broken the images, speech and transcription calls that share this client.

evidence.detail: check --run on a driver that exercises chat, streamed chat, summarise, vision and streamed vision: 5 of 5 requests reached router-sim as valid /v1/responses with model=gpt-4o, and the driver's own assertions on each answer passed
same driver with enable_functions=True and two plugins loaded: 5 of 5 valid, so the legacy functions/function_call payload translates cleanly
compileall plus importing openai_helper, plugin_manager, telegram_bot and main: 5 passed, same as the baseline
no migration key was present in this environment (check --run --live reported 'no migration key'), so every Router request was verified against the local simulator only

items.title: Images, speech and transcription stay on OpenAI
items.summary: DALL-E image generation, TTS and Whisper transcription keep going to OpenAI directly, because Router serves no image, audio or files endpoint.
items.gains: nothing: these three features keep working exactly as before
items.loses: These three features are not on Router, so the OPENAI_API_KEY must stay configured and their spend is not visible in Router's per-key reporting. /image, /tts and voice-message transcription are therefore the part of the bot a Router outage cannot protect and a Router dashboard cannot account for.
items.why: Router's endpoint list has /v1/responses, /v1/messages, count_tokens and /v1/models; /v1/images/generations and the audio endpoints return a plain-text 404. The runtime recognises these calls and leaves them on the provider untouched, which is the correct outcome rather than a workaround: there is nothing to route them to. They share the same wrapped client as the chat calls, so no extra client or key handling was needed. Worth flagging to whoever sizes the Router key's spend cap: image, TTS and transcription cost will keep appearing on the OpenAI bill.

evidence.detail: router-migrate check --all: these three sites report 'stays: hard limit — Router has no endpoint for it'; the other four report ROUTES

items.title: Survive provider failure on the chat path
items.summary: A router.policy.json gives the chat, vision, function-call and summarise features a provider timeout, a cache key and a cross-vendor fallback list.
items.gains: A 429 or an OpenAI-side failure before the first token is answered by gpt-4.1-mini, or by claude-haiku-4-5 if OpenAI is down as a whole, instead of entering the hand-rolled tenacity loop that sleeps 20 seconds and retries the same model up to three times: today a rate-limited user waits up to 40 seconds of pure sleep and then sees an error, and a provider hang can hold the request for the SDK's 600-second default. The policy caps a provider call at 60 seconds (30 for summarisation) and keeps the conversation's prefix on one provider via prompt_cache_key. The fallback candidates are also cheaper than the primary ($0.40/$1.60 and $1/$5 per 1M against gpt-4o's $2.50/$10), so a degraded answer is a cheaper answer.
items.loses: On a fallback the reply comes from a different model, so answers will differ and the bot never says so; the response's token counts (which the bot shows with SHOW_USAGE and bills against user budgets) are then for whichever model served. Router does not fall back once a stream has started, so with the default STREAM=true this only covers failures before the first token. Setting fallbacks replaces the single `model` with a candidate list, which also means Flex cannot apply to these requests (gpt-4o has no Flex tier anyway).
items.price: No change on the happy path. On a fallback, gpt-4.1-mini is 84% cheaper per input token and claude-haiku-4-5 60% cheaper than gpt-4o; a truncated first attempt is still billed.
items.why: This bot's only answer to provider trouble is a tenacity decorator that catches RateLimitError, sleeps a fixed 20 seconds and tries the identical request against the identical model — the one strategy that cannot work when the problem is that model's capacity, and the worst possible experience for someone watching a Telegram chat. It also does nothing at all for a 5xx or a hang. Router's fallback list is the right mechanism because the alternative, another model, is exactly what a rate limit calls for, and it is a configuration change rather than code: the policy applies only to Router-bound requests, so the direct-to-OpenAI path keeps its original behaviour. I kept the tenacity decorator in place; it now only fires if Router itself returns 429, which is the case it was always right for.

evidence.detail: check --run on the five-path driver with the policy compiled: 5 of 5 valid, every request now sent with a candidate list instead of a single model (the simulator logs model=None), and all five driver assertions still passed
compileall plus the four module imports: 5 passed on the branch
no migration key available; fallback behaviour on a real provider outage is documented by Router but unmeasured even upstream

items.title: Summarise chat history with a cheap model
items.summary: A policy model_map sends only the summarisation feature to gpt-4o-mini, leaving every user-facing answer on gpt-4o.
items.gains: About 94% off every summarisation call ($0.15/$0.60 per 1M against $2.50/$10), and a faster one: on a long conversation this call blocks the user's reply, because __common_get_chat_response summarises the history inline before it asks for the answer. A typical summarise of a 15-message history costs roughly $0.0095 on gpt-4o and $0.0006 on gpt-4o-mini. It fires on every turn once a chat passes MAX_HISTORY_SIZE, so for a talkative chat it is a per-turn tax.
items.loses: Answers will differ: summaries will be blunter, and because the summary becomes the chat's new history, a worse summary slightly degrades the following answers. The map is keyed on the configured model (gpt-4o, gpt-4.1, gpt-4-turbo), so an operator who sets OPENAI_MODEL to something else keeps paying full price for summaries until the map learns that id.
items.price: -94% per summarisation call; no change to any other call.
items.why: Compressing a conversation into 700 characters is the most mechanical thing this bot asks a model to do, and it is the only call whose output no user ever reads directly. Paying the flagship rate for it buys very little, and paying it in the middle of someone's reply costs latency too. Doing this as a policy model_map rather than a code change matters here: the app's token accounting, context-window table and vision checks are all hard-coded around config['model'], so changing that value in code would walk into __max_model_tokens's NotImplementedError. The map swaps the id on the wire for one feature and leaves all of that alone.

evidence.detail: check --run on the five-path driver: the __summarise request arrived as model=gpt-4o-mini and the four chat/vision requests as model=gpt-4o, exactly the intended split; all driver assertions passed
live catalog: gpt-4o $2.50/$10, gpt-4o-mini $0.15/$0.60 per 1M input/output tokens
compileall plus the four module imports: passed on the branch
no migration key, so summary quality on the two models was not compared; nothing offline measures it

items.title: Key the prompt cache per conversation
items.summary: Chat, vision and function-call requests carry prompt_cache_key=chat-<id> when Router is on, so each conversation reuses one cached prefix.
items.gains: Every turn of a chat resends the same system prompt and the same growing history, which is exactly the shape prompt caching pays for. A cached prefix is billed at gpt-4o's cache-read rate of $1.25 instead of $2.50 per 1M input tokens, so on a long chat the input half of the bill roughly halves; keying on the chat rather than on the feature also keeps one conversation on one provider, which is what makes the hit rate hold up. It matters more if the chat model is ever pointed at Claude, which Router measured as not caching at all without a key and 90% cheaper with one.
items.price: Up to -50% on the cached part of gpt-4o input tokens; no extra charge for the key itself and no behaviour change.
items.why: This is the cheapest lever available to a bot whose whole request shape is a repeated prefix plus one new user message. The helper returns nothing unless RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY is set, so the direct-to-OpenAI path is byte-identical to before and there is no question of OpenAI rejecting the field. A request's own prompt_cache_key wins over the policy's, so this composes with i1 rather than fighting it: approve both and the per-chat key is the one used. Caching only pays above roughly 1,024 identical leading tokens, so short chats see nothing, which is the right side to fail on.

evidence.detail: check --run on the five-path driver: 5 of 5 valid /v1/responses, all driver assertions passed

the runtime's chat-to-responses translator copies prompt_cache_key straight from the chat body into the Responses body (bot/router_runtime.py:232), and the policy only fills it in when the request has none (bot/router_runtime.py:479)
live catalog: gpt-4o cache_read_input $1.25 against input $2.50 per 1M
compileall plus the four module imports: passed on the branch

items.title: Bill users from Router's reported cost
items.summary: Replace usage_tracker's flat TOKEN_PRICE arithmetic with the exact usage.cost Router returns on every Responses call.
items.gains: Per-user budgets become true. Today the tracker multiplies total tokens by TOKEN_PRICE, default $0.002 per 1K, which is a 2023 gpt-3.5 number applied to gpt-4o traffic and applied to input and output at one rate when gpt-4o charges four times more for output. A chat-heavy user is therefore under-billed against their USER_BUDGETS cap, the /stats figures are wrong in the same direction, and the error grows with every model change. Router reports usage.cost in USD on /v1/responses and it matched list price exactly in Router's own checks, so the number can simply be recorded instead of estimated. It would also make the vision tracker's separate VISION_TOKEN_PRICE, a flat $0.01 per 1K, unnecessary.
items.loses: Recorded costs change, so users' accumulated spend and their position against GUEST_BUDGET/USER_BUDGETS shifts the moment it ships (upward, for the default settings), and stored usage logs mix two accounting methods. Image, TTS and transcription spend still has to be estimated the old way because those calls never reach Router (s1), and the OpenAI fallback path returns no cost either, so the estimator cannot be deleted, only demoted to a fallback. Reaching usage.cost means the chat path has to see the Responses body rather than the translated chat-shaped response, which pushes this towards i6.
items.price: No change in what is spent; a correction to what is recorded.
items.why: This bot enforces money limits on its users with a hard-coded guess at what a token costs, and the guess is now off by several times. Once traffic is on Router the right number arrives in every response for free. I did not build it because it changes figures users can see and budgets that may already be tuned around the current under-counting, and because getting at the cost field cleanly depends on how the chat path talks to Router (i6) rather than on the tracker alone.

evidence.detail: bot/usage_tracker.py:75 bills chat at tokens * 0.002 / 1000 and :160 vision at tokens * 0.01 / 1000; Router reports usage.cost per request on /v1/responses only

items.title: Pick model limits from Router's live catalog
items.summary: Replace the hard-coded 2024 OpenAI model tables with Router's /v1/models, so any catalog model can be configured and works.
items.gains: Right now OPENAI_MODEL can only be one of about twenty ids frozen into GPT_3_MODELS through O_MODELS in bot/openai_helper.py. Set it to claude-sonnet-5, gemini-3.8-flash or gpt-5.4-mini, all of which Router serves, and the bot crashes in __max_model_tokens's NotImplementedError or miscounts tokens in __count_tokens. Router's catalog reports max_output_tokens, tools, temperature support and input_modalities for each of 75 non-BYOK ids, which is precisely what those four tables try to hard-code. Driving them from the catalog turns the model into a real configuration knob: the operator could run the whole bot on claude-haiku-5-5 at $0.10/$0.50 per 1M, 96% below gpt-4o, or on a reasoning model, without touching code. It would also delete are_functions_available's stale list and the gpt-4o-only assumption in __count_tokens_vision.
items.loses: The model tables become a network dependency: the catalog has to be fetched (and cached, with a shipped fallback) at startup, where today the answer is a tuple lookup. tiktoken only counts OpenAI tokenisations, so for a non-OpenAI model the history-length trigger and the token figures shown to users need another source, Router's free /v1/messages/count_tokens being the exact one for Claude and an estimate elsewhere; token counts users see would change slightly. The hard-coded guards currently fail loudly on an unknown model, which is crude but safe, and a catalog-driven version will instead try to serve it.
items.price: No change by itself. It is what makes the cheaper models in the catalog reachable at all.
items.why: This is the one thing I would build differently if the bot were starting on Router today. All of its model knowledge is a 2024 snapshot of one vendor's price list, copied into four separate tables that each raise NotImplementedError when reality moves, and the vendor dimension does not exist at all. Router already publishes the same facts for every model it serves, on both API surfaces, so the tables are not just stale but redundant. It needs a conversation, not a patch: it touches token accounting, the summarisation trigger, the vision path and what users are billed, and its payoff is a product decision about which model this bot should run on.

evidence.detail: live catalog: 100 ids, 75 without BYOK, each with max_output_tokens, tools, temperature and input_modalities; bot/openai_helper.py:39-74 and :619-716 hard-code the same facts for about twenty OpenAI ids and raise NotImplementedError otherwise

items.title: Port the chat path to the Responses API
items.summary: Call /v1/responses directly instead of chat.completions through the runtime's translator, so the per-request Router levers apply inline.
items.gains: Every Router lever is a Responses field, and today the chat path can only reach them through router.policy.json because the code speaks Chat Completions. Calling Responses directly would let the bot set fallback_timeout on a streamed request, the one lever that helps the default STREAM=true path (Router cannot fall back once a stream has started, but it will if the first token is late: Router measured a fallback at a 2-second deadline), set metadata per Telegram user so Router's spend views break down by who is talking, read usage.cost per request (i4), choose a service tier or Flex per feature, and pass reasoning effort on the models that have it. It also removes a translation layer from the path of every user-visible reply and would replace the legacy `functions` payload, which OpenAI deprecated, with tools.
items.loses: A real rewrite of the three response-handling paths in openai_helper.py and the streaming consumer in telegram_bot.py, which reads chunk.choices[0].delta today and would read Responses events instead. The chat path would no longer run against a plain OpenAI key through the same code unless both request shapes are kept, so the per-request provider fallback the runtime gives for free either goes away or has to be hand-written. n_choices, which Responses has no field for, would have to be emulated or dropped (see n1), and the plugin function-call loop would be rebuilt against tools. Output could differ in small ways wherever the translation is not exactly equivalent.
items.price: No change by itself; it is the prerequisite for the Flex tier (up to -50% on an eligible model) and for exact cost accounting.
items.why: The migration deliberately kept the app's request shape, which was right for getting traffic onto Router safely in one commit. But the shape it kept is a 2023 Chat Completions call with legacy `functions`, and every lever worth having on Router lives on the other surface. The honest version of this is: if this bot were written against Router today, openai_helper would be a Responses client, and the policy file would be a convenience rather than the only way to reach a timeout or a fallback. Worth doing once the fallback and caching work above has shown what the chat path actually needs.

evidence.detail: fallback_timeout requires stream=true and at least two candidates and is a Responses-only field; the bot streams by default (STREAM=true in bot/main.py:36) and reaches Router today only through the runtime's Chat Completions translation

items.title: Two settings silently take chat off Router
items.summary: N_CHOICES above 1 or PRESENCE_PENALTY away from 0 makes the runtime keep every chat request on OpenAI, with no error.
items.gains: Deciding this is what makes the migration's coverage stable rather than dependent on one operator's .env.
items.loses: Either the two settings lose their effect, or that deployment's chat traffic is not on Router.
items.why: The bot sends `n` and `presence_penalty` on every chat request. Router's Responses API rejects both (`n` outright; a non-zero presence_penalty is not accepted), so the runtime correctly keeps those requests on the provider rather than changing their meaning — which means a deployment with N_CHOICES=2 or PRESENCE_PENALTY=0.5 routes none of its chat traffic and nobody is told. Three ways out, and it is a product call which: drop the parameters on Router-bound requests only (router-migrate adapt --drop presence_penalty, losing the penalty's effect on wording while keeping the traffic routed); emulate n_choices with parallel single-choice requests, which is also the only way it could ever work alongside streaming, since the streaming path already ignores the extra choices; or declare both settings unsupported and fail at startup instead of silently leaving the gateway. My recommendation is to drop presence_penalty on the Router path and to retire N_CHOICES, which the default (1) and the streaming path already treat as dead weight.

evidence.detail: bot/router_runtime.py:174 and :184 keep a request on the provider when presence_penalty is non-zero or n != 1; bot/openai_helper.py sends both on every chat request from bot/main.py's N_CHOICES and PRESENCE_PENALTY defaults (1 and 0.0, which do route)

items.title: A custom OPENAI_BASE_URL bypasses Router
items.summary: The OpenAI SDK picks up OPENAI_BASE_URL from the environment, and the runtime only routes OpenAI's own host, so a deployment pointed at a proxy routes nothing.
items.why: .env.example advertises OPENAI_BASE_URL, and openai.AsyncOpenAI reads it without the app's involvement, so a deployment behind a compatible proxy or an Azure-style endpoint keeps every chat request off Router even with RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY set. That is the runtime behaving correctly rather than a defect, and for the default deployment it is a non-issue. If such a deployment exists, the runtime takes an unlock_hosts list for another vendor's OpenAI-compatible host, which would route its catalog-model traffic; ROUTER_MIGRATE_TRACE=<file> is the quick way to confirm where a given deployment's requests actually go.

evidence.detail: .env.example documents OPENAI_BASE_URL; bot/openai_helper.py:113 passes no base_url, so the SDK's env default applies
